newsitem.title: FRANCE: French unions renew protests, but turnout low.
newsitem.headline: French unions renew protests, but turnout low.

text.p: French workers renewed their street protests on Saturday against unpopular government welfare reforms, but in much smaller numbers than trade union leaders hoped for.
In Rennes, northern France, just 2,500 people marched compared with 10,000 in a similar protest last year.

In the southern port city Marseille, just 3,000 people turned up, according to police, although organisers said the number was closer to 10,000. In Toulouse, southern France, 2,500 to 3,500 marched, police and organisers said.
Saturday's protests were called to coincide with the first anniversary of a controversial welfare reform plan unveiled by conservative Prime Minister Alain Juppe on November 15, 1995.

Juppe's approval rating hit a record low of 25 percent this week in a Gallup poll for the weekly L'Express, but protests were far smaller than a year ago, when transport and public sector strikes virtually paralysed France for weeks.

Despite the low turnout, the leader of the Communist-led CGT union pledged to organise a further day of national action in coming weeks in protest against government austerity policies during a time of record unemployment.

CGT secretary general Louis Viannet, marching in the central city Aurillac, said new demonstrations across France were needed because of "a system which is leading to more and more pressure on our finances".
But Marc Blondel, leader of the more moderate Force Ouvriere union, said Viannet was acting on his own and urged unions to determine clear common goals before planning more demonstrations.
"I don't believe in unity for unity's sake," said Blondel, who was marching in Paris.
The two crossed swords over strategy a day after a public transport strike called for Paris failed to materialise.

Transport union leaders had hoped that Friday's strike would paralyse the capital and thus crown a week of protests in favour of wage increases and against job cuts and privatisations with unemployment at 12.6 percent in September.
But city transport officials said Paris commuter services ran at near-normal levels throughout the day as union members failed to heed their leaders' call for action.

However a strike by pilots' unions at Air France Europe, part of the Air France group, entered its second and final day on Saturday and succeeded in grounding half of the carrier's scheduled flights, airline officials said.
The 48-hour strike called by the USPNT, SPIT, SNPNAC and SPNL unions was intended to protest at planned job cuts.
